issues.quote: Then a man from the book shop came. "This boy did not take it," he said. / The old man was Mr. Brownlow.
issues.problem: The last 'man' mentioned is the man from the book shop, so 'The old man was Mr. Brownlow' reads as if the book-shop man is Mr. Brownlow. At A1 the text never says the robbed old man is in the court, so learners will likely mix up the two men.
issues.fix: Start the last paragraph with: "The old man from the street was there too. His name was Mr. Brownlow."

issues.quote: Every day they got one small bowl.
issues.problem: This says the children ate only one bowl a day. B2 and C1 (and the original) have thin porridge three times a day, so the levels contradict each other.
issues.fix: "At every meal they got one small bowl."

notes: Charley is named ("Oliver went out with the Dodger and Charley.") but never introduced. Consider "Oliver went out with the Dodger and another boy, Charley."
Mr. Sowerberry appears without any setup after the dark room. Consider adding "Then a man took Oliver away." or similar.

"They locked Oliver in the cellar and sent for Mr. Bumble. Early the next morning, Oliver opened the door and left." could suggest that he simply walked out of a locked cellar. Consider "That night they let him out and he slept in the shop. Early the next morning..."
Mr. Bumble is named without being introduced ("he shouted for Mr. Bumble"). Adding "a man of the workhouse" would help.

issues.quote: Every day, each boy received one small bowl of thin porridge, and nothing more.
issues.problem: This states one bowl per day. B2 and C1 (and the original) have thin porridge three times a day, so this contradicts the other levels and the source.
issues.fix: "At every meal, each boy received one small bowl of thin porridge, and nothing more."

notes: "the boy would end badly" is slightly unidiomatic. "would come to a bad end" is the natural phrase and fits B1.
B1 and B2 have Oliver faint on the court floor, while C1 has him faint 'on the stones outside'. Both are defensible from the original, but aligning them would be tidier.
"Oliver, however, was beyond hearing it" has a vague referent ('it' = the magistrate's ungracious release). Consider "was beyond hearing any of it".
"filled with remorse" is a little strong for Brownlow. "filled with pity and some guilt" may fit the original better. Taste only.

summary: The story follows Dickens closely at every level: the lots, the white-waistcoat gentleman, the five-pound notice, Noah, the 'meat not madness' joke, the milestone, Barnet, Fagin's box and game, the bookstall, Fang and the fever at Brownlow's. It is gentle enough for 4+ and avoids caricaturing Fagin. A1 and B1 say the boys got one bowl a day, which contradicts B2/C1 and the original, and A1's ending makes it unclear whether the book-shop man is Mr. Brownlow.
